info.name: Wholesale B2B — Customer API v1
info.description:
Read API over the same catalog you see when you sign in to the website.

## Set this up in 30 seconds

1. Open the collection's **Variables** tab.
2. Set `baseUrl` to your store's address, e.g. `https://example.com` (no trailing slash).
3. Set `apiKey` to the key from **My Profile › My API Key** on the site.
4. Send **Catalog › List products**.

Authentication is set once at the collection level, so every request inherits it — you never paste the key into an individual request.

## The one thing to understand

**Your key is you.** A request authenticates as your own user account and then runs through the same code the website runs. You see your company's prices, your company's products, your fulfillment region, and nothing you could not see by logging in. A colleague's key can legitimately return different prices and a different product list from the identical request.

That also means an administrator switching your access off takes effect on your next call, and switching it back on makes your existing key work again — there is nothing to regenerate.

## Keep the key in the header

The API accepts the key only as an `X-Api-Key` header, never in the URL, so it cannot leak into browser history, `Referer` headers or server access logs. Postman is configured that way below; please keep it that way.

## Limits

60 requests per minute per key. Over that you get `429` with a `Retry-After` header telling you how many seconds to wait — read it rather than retrying blind.

Full reference: `docs/api/openapi.yaml` in the product repository, or ask your administrator for the OpenAPI file.

Run this one with Postman's **Collection Runner** (or Run folder) — on its own it fetches a single page.

It sets `cursorPage` itself and re-queues itself until `page` reaches `pages`, collecting every product into the `allProducts` variable. That is the whole pagination pattern: there are no cursors or tokens, just `page` and `pages`.

item.name: Troubleshooting
item.description:
What each refusal looks like, so you can recognise one from its response instead of guessing.

The status codes are deliberately distinct: `401` means we could not identify you, `403` means we did and the answer is still no, `400` means the request needs one more parameter, `429` means slow down.

request.description: Overrides the collection auth to send nothing. Expect `401 {"error": "Missing X-Api-Key header."}`.

exec: pm.test('401 with a readable reason', function () {

request.description: `Invalid API key.` and `This API key has been revoked.` are separate messages on purpose — the first means you typed it wrong, the second means it was yours and you turned it off. Regenerate from My Profile › My API Key.

A valid key being refused. The message says whether it is your company's access or your own that was switched off, because those are different people to go and ask. Nothing needs regenerating — re-enabling makes this same key work again.
